before_questions: Am I trying to solve the problem, or prove that I'm right?
What am I avoiding saying because it's uncomfortable?
What part of this have I contributed to?
Am I confusing accountability with punishment?
Can I hold a high standard and genuinely want this person to succeed?

awareness.name: Awareness
awareness.healthy: People examine their own assumptions and contribution before diagnosing others.
awareness.warning: Blame increases. Defensiveness increases. The same problem keeps happening despite repeated attempts to fix other people.
awareness.pattern: The organization is treating problems as something other people have rather than something the system is producing.
awareness.move: Before solving the problem, examine your own role in creating or maintaining it.
awareness.ask: What might I be contributing that I can't currently see?

trust.name: Trust
trust.tag: Create the conditions for people to do their best work.
trust.healthy: People tell the truth, ask for help, challenge ideas, take risks, and recover from mistakes.
trust.warning: People stay quiet in meetings. Problems surface late. Everyone agrees publicly and disagrees privately.
trust.pattern: People are managing their relationship with authority rather than focusing entirely on the work.
trust.move: Reward candor, especially when the information is uncomfortable.
trust.ask: What truth are people least likely to tell me?

conditions.name: Conditions
conditions.tag: Design the environment, not just the behavior.
conditions.healthy: The environment makes the desired behavior relatively easy and the right priorities visible.
conditions.warning: People are constantly told to communicate better, take ownership, or prioritize, but the system keeps producing the opposite.
conditions.pattern: The organization is trying to change people without changing the conditions around them.
conditions.move: Change the environment that produces the behavior.
conditions.ask: What are our current conditions making almost inevitable?

value.name: Value
value.healthy: People understand who they serve, what matters to them, and how their work contributes to the outcome.
value.warning: More activity, more meetings, more reports, but little movement in meaningful outcomes.
value.pattern: Activity has become a proxy for value.
value.move: Trace work all the way to the customer or business outcome.
value.ask: If we stopped doing this, who would actually lose value?

incentives.name: Incentives
incentives.tag: Look at what the system actually rewards.
incentives.healthy: The behaviors that get rewarded are broadly aligned with what the organization says it values.
incentives.warning: People optimize metrics, protect their territory, avoid risk, or pursue short-term wins despite the stated strategy.
incentives.pattern: The real strategy is being communicated through consequences, not words.
incentives.move: Examine what gets rewarded, promoted, measured, celebrated, and tolerated.
incentives.ask: What behavior are we unintentionally paying people to produce?

leverage.name: Leverage
leverage.healthy: A decision, process improvement, relationship, or coaching intervention improves outcomes far beyond the initial effort.
leverage.warning: Leaders are busy everywhere but progress is slow. More people and more effort aren't producing proportional results.
leverage.pattern: Effort is being applied to symptoms instead of constraints or high-leverage points.
leverage.move: Find the point where changing one thing changes many things.
leverage.ask: Where would one hour of attention create the greatest downstream impact?

rescue.name: Rescuing
rescue.coach: You step in and fix it, or give the answer before you have asked. It works today and teaches the team to wait for you.

avoid.name: Avoiding
avoid.coach: You wait, soften, or hand it off. The conversation you skip is usually the one that matters.

control.name: Controlling
control.coach: You reach for a rule, a check or a consequence where a conversation would do.

please.name: Pleasing
please.coach: You protect how people feel about you, or decide what they can handle.

promise.name: Over-promising
promise.coach: You commit, or cheer a commitment, past what the evidence supports.

blame.name: Defending
blame.coach: You explain or point elsewhere before saying what is yours.

grind.name: Grinding
grind.coach: You answer pressure with more hours and call it dedication.

narrow.name: One explanation
narrow.coach: You settle on the first story that fits and stop looking.

standard.name: Standards
standard.blurb: Say what good looks like, and hold it for everyone.
standard.strong: You set the bar in plain words and hold it, including for people you like.
standard.watch: You let a standard bend for people you like or numbers you need.

candor.name: Candor
candor.blurb: Say the true thing, early, and kindly.
candor.strong: You say the hard thing early and plainly, and stay kind.
candor.watch: You soften or delay the hard thing until it is harder.

system.name: Systems
system.blurb: Build it so results don't depend on a hero.
system.strong: You fix the process, not just the problem.
system.watch: You fix it yourself, or lean on the one person who delivers.

trust.name: Trust and verify
trust.blurb: Give trust freely. Check what matters, the same way for everyone.
trust.strong: You trust the person and check the work, and say so.
trust.watch: You take confidence for evidence, or check people in ways they feel.

self.name: Leading yourself
self.blurb: Own your reactions, your fears and your rest.
self.strong: You name your part first and protect the rest you need.
self.watch: You defend, push through, or hold on to the work you love.

across.name: Up and across
across.blurb: Carry the truth up, the context down, and a fair view sideways.
across.strong: You bring the range, the drivers and the ask.
across.watch: You promise upward, stay quiet across, or see only your own function.

grow.name: Growing people
grow.blurb: Ask first. Help them get better, not just get it done.
grow.strong: You ask before you answer and stay beside people as they decide.
grow.watch: You answer fast, rescue, or take the quiet for the answer.

cases.principle: Delayed kindness is a loan she repays with interest.

tension.lesson: Take responsibility for your part.

cases.pause: What did Lena hear in “next cycle”? What did you mean?
cases.principle: A vague promise is a debt. Pay it with specifics.
cases.next_move: List every “next cycle” you've said. Make each a date or a no.
cases.strong_move: Tell her now: not this cycle, and here's why.

tension.lesson: Helping people perform can mean being slower today.

cases.pause: Whose proposal is this, and what does the team learn?
cases.principle: Weekly fixes are a process problem, not a favor.
cases.next_move: List the last five things you fixed. Write a checklist for the commonest.
cases.strong_move: Sit with her at the keyboard and fix this one together.

lens.lesson: Strong outcomes shouldn't depend on one person.

tension.lesson: Trust built over years earns the right to ask for more.

cases.pause: Is it loyal to leave him carrying this alone?
cases.principle: One-person dependence isn't loyalty. It's a risk he carries alone.
cases.next_move: List your five biggest accounts and who else could run each.
cases.strong_move: Ask Sam to design his own backup, starting with why.

lens.book: What the CEO Wants You to Know
lens.lesson: Know what drives profit and cash before celebrating a number.

tension.lesson: Pay shapes behavior; bring psychology and economics.

cases.pause: What does telling your director now risk, and what does waiting risk?
cases.principle: People do what the number pays for. Fix yours first.
cases.next_move: For each number you pay on, ask how a clever rep could game it.
cases.strong_move: Ask your director to pay you on retail, not shipments.

lens.lesson: Give people context to decide without waiting for permission.

tension.lesson: Useful metrics let you check what was decided.

cases.pause: What are you protecting by approving $900?
cases.principle: Give context and a limit, not permission case by case.
cases.next_move: Ask a rep what they skipped for fear of not being allowed.
cases.strong_move: Give everyone the budget and a $2,000 limit.

lens.lesson: Ask good questions and give honest feedback, so the truth reaches you.

tension.lesson: Clear expectations and useful metrics apply to everyone.

cases.pause: Can you check his work without him hearing that you doubt him?
cases.principle: Trust the person, check the work, check everyone alike.
cases.next_move: Pick one status you accept on someone's word. Spot-check it.
cases.strong_move: Visit two stores and ask which were hardest.

lens.lesson: Statistics and incentives keep a confident story from passing as the whole picture.

tension.lesson: Building trust helps talented people do their best.

cases.pause: Would Dave bet his own money on it?
cases.principle: Confidence is a feeling. Evidence is what the buyer did.
cases.next_move: Tally each rep's “locks” against closes. Show them quarterly.
cases.strong_move: Count Safeway at half until the buyer sets a date.

lens.lesson: Build an environment where speaking up is safe.

tension.lesson: More perspectives keep you from missing the whole picture.

cases.pause: What does disagreeing with you cost a rep?
cases.principle: Silence isn't agreement. Ask what disagreeing with you costs.
cases.next_move: Ask “what's the weakest part of this plan?” and wait.
cases.strong_move: Reopen the plan by owning how you cut off pushback.

lens.lesson: Check economics, incentives and behavior before settling on a story about a person.

tension.lesson: Stay curious; notice when ego writes the story.

cases.pause: What would you see if it weren't effort?
cases.principle: Before you explain a person, rule out the situation.
cases.next_move: When numbers move, list three causes that aren't the person.
cases.strong_move: Check her numbers against the re-cut and pay plan.

lens.lesson: How you show up while getting results matters as much as the results.

tension.lesson: A team with context can carry some of the load.

cases.pause: What would you tell a friend running on five hours' sleep?
cases.principle: Tired is a business risk. Protect rest like a key account.
cases.next_move: Block next week's non-negotiables first: sleep, one evening, one meal.
cases.strong_move: Sleep seven hours a night until the 31st.

lens.lesson: Take responsibility, and notice when defensiveness drives you.

tension.lesson: A good leader welcomes honest feedback.

cases.pause: What would your best rep say first?
cases.principle: Own it in one sentence before you explain it.
cases.next_move: Write the one sentence you'd say after a miss.
cases.strong_move: Say: “I championed this program, and it missed.”

lens.lesson: A manager creates leverage by developing the people around them.

tension.lesson: How you show up matters; notice what drives you.

cases.pause: Who pays when your hours go to what you love?
cases.principle: Keep what you love, and use it to make someone better.
cases.next_move: Book the two overdue one-on-ones first.
cases.strong_move: Keep one store morning a month, with a rep leading.

lens.lesson: Give people context and autonomy so they act without permission.

tension.lesson: Notice whether your reaction serves the work or your ego.

cases.pause: If you never replied, who would decide?
cases.principle: Rest works when the team knows who decides.
cases.next_move: Before time off, write who decides what and who covers.
cases.strong_move: Reply once: “Inside your limit. Your call.”

lens.lesson: More perspectives and statistics keep a familiar pattern from passing as the whole picture.

tension.lesson: Ask good questions so the team can improve the plan.

cases.pause: What would show you were wrong in 30 days?
cases.principle: When you're most sure, look hardest for how you're wrong.
cases.next_move: Before a big plan, write what you'd see in 30 days if wrong.
cases.strong_move: Pilot 15% of effort in three markets for six weeks.

lens.lesson: Stay curious and own your reaction.

tension.lesson: Context helps people decide, and a request's purpose is context.

cases.pause: What is the deadline for? Do you know?
cases.principle: Ask what a deadline is for before giving up a weekend.
cases.next_move: When a deadline lands late, ask what decision it supports.
cases.strong_move: Reply: “What decision does Monday make?”

loops.source: Matthew Schmidt site, The Blind Spot section and its modal (variable loopStages). Copy is the owner's own, quoted as written.
loops.intro: Sometimes the hardest thing to see is what everyone has learned to accept.

activity.name: The Activity Loop
activity.heading: More activity. Same problem.
activity.text: More data, more decks, more meetings. Information moves, presentations multiply, meetings repeat. Yet decisions stall, the same issues return, and the organization risks confusing the visibility of work with its impact.
activity.blind_spot: Activity can look like progress yet results remain unchanged.

learning.name: The Learning Loop
learning.heading: Signal becomes understanding.
learning.text: A loop where every decision makes the next one better. Actions generate outcomes, and outcomes create learning that shapes what happens next.
learning.advantage: Each cycle builds on the last, turning better decisions into better results over time.

insight.heading: The Difference Is What Happens Next.
insight.text: It's not the amount of activity that creates progress. It's whether that activity changes what happens next. Information must change understanding. Understanding must inform decisions. Decisions must lead to action. And action must generate learning that improves the next cycle. One loop repeats the work. The other builds on it.
insight.final: That's the difference between staying busy and getting better.

loops.teamwork_use: A hard conversation can be activity (the same argument again) or learning (a stated expectation, a dated check, a lesson kept). Teamwork is built so that every pass ends in a written expectation and a look-back, which is the only thing that turns the second conversation into something other than a repeat of the first.

lenses.source: Matthew Schmidt site, The Three Lenses section and its modal (variable vennStages). Copy is the owner's own, quoted as written.
lenses.rule: Look at the same situation three ways: how the business creates value, how the system creates leverage, and how people are helped to do their best work.

business.heading: Create Value
business.text: Every organization exists to create value. The question is whether its strategy, priorities, and measures of success are aligned around the value that matters most.
business.blind_spot: Optimizing individual results without understanding how they contribute to the whole.
business.connection: Business defines the value to pursue. Systems determine how that value can be delivered, and people bring it to life.

system.heading: Create Leverage
system.text: A system determines how work flows, how decisions get made, and how effort translates into results. The right system makes it easier for people to create value consistently.
system.blind_spot: Expecting better results from people while leaving the conditions that shape their work unchanged.
system.connection: Systems turn business intent into an operating reality. Their effectiveness depends on both the value they serve and the people working within them.

people.heading: Create Capability
people.text: People bring the judgment, knowledge, creativity, and ability that turn strategy and systems into real outcomes. Their potential is realized when they have the clarity, support, and conditions to do their best work.
people.blind_spot: Expecting people to compensate indefinitely for systems that make good performance difficult.
people.connection: People give the organization its capability to act, adapt, and improve. What they can accomplish depends on how the business and system enable them.

leadership.heading: A clear direction only matters when it changes what the organization does.
leadership.text: Connecting business direction with the systems and decisions that turn intent into action.

capability.heading: Potential becomes performance when people have the conditions to apply what they know.
capability.text: Connecting people's abilities with the systems, tools, and conditions that enable effective performance.

scale.heading: Growth becomes sustainable when the organization can reproduce results without reproducing the same problems.
scale.text: Connecting value creation, repeatable systems, and human capability so results can grow without depending on heroic individual effort.

multiplier.heading: The whole is greater when the parts work together.
multiplier.text: Business defines the value worth creating. Systems make that value repeatable. People bring the capability to deliver it.
multiplier.final: The question isn't whether your business, systems, and people are strong individually. It's whether they're making one another stronger.

lenses.teamwork_use: The three lenses are why the advisor always carries a cause that is not about anyone's character. A situation read only through People produces blame; read only through Business it produces pressure; read only through System it can excuse conduct. Teamwork holds all three open until a fact rules one out.

path.source: Matthew Schmidt site, The Path to Agency section. Copy is the owner's own.
path.heading: The Path to Agency
path.tagline: The Path helps you see beneath the complexity.
path.text: Complexity becomes clearer when we learn to see the patterns and relationships that shape it. Complex problems rarely yield to a single perspective. The lenses help us see, the forces help us understand, the ideas that follow help us develop better judgment, and judgment is what turns knowledge into agency.

knowledge.teamwork: What happened, what was told, what was concluded: sorted and checked with the person.

understanding.teamwork: Two or three readings held open, including one about the setup, with the fact that would tell them apart.

judgment.teamwork: One next step with its assumption, its risk and an alternative, chosen by the person.

agency.teamwork: The person acts, writes what they expect, and later compares it with what happened.

path.forces_note: The six forces (Awareness, Trust, Conditions, Value, Incentives, Leverage) are the website's ideaData cards and live in `forces`.

friction_section.title: The Friction
friction_section.lead: The strategy is sound. So why aren't the results there?
body: The priorities are set. The processes are in place. The people are capable.
And yet, progress stalls. The same problems return. Results depend on constant intervention.
Something is getting lost between what the organization intends and what it actually delivers.
friction_section.room_line: Friction is the symptom. The Gap is Where To Focus.
friction_section.teamwork_use: In one person's situation the gap is between what was intended, said or promised and what then happened. Teamwork asks the person to name both ends in observable words, then looks at what sits between them.

books_takeaways.source: Matthew Schmidt site, Reading section ('Books That Shaped How I Lead'): the card line, and the modal behind 'Read the takeaway'. The network section's core-idea lines are included as `network_core_idea`. All of it is the owner's reading of the books. None of it is a quotation from the books.

items.title: How Google Works
items.author: Eric Schmidt & Jonathan Rosenberg
items.card_line: The environments we create matter as much as who we hire. Transparency, autonomy, and context help people act without waiting for permission.
items.takeaway: How Google Works made me think more deeply about the environments we create for people. Hiring well matters, but so do transparency, autonomy, psychological safety, and giving people enough context to make good decisions without waiting for permission.
items.network_core_idea: Outcomes are shaped by the environment around people. Culture, information, autonomy, incentives, talent, and decision-making systems determine what an organization is capable of. Don't just manage the output. Design the conditions that produce it.
items.teamwork_role: Conditions vocabulary for the setup explanation: context over control, transparency, decision rights.

items.title: The 15 Commitments of Conscious Leadership
items.author: Dethmer, Chapman & Klemp
items.card_line: Leadership is as much about how you show up, staying curious and owning your reactions, as what you actually accomplish.
items.takeaway: The 15 Commitments of Conscious Leadership challenged me to look at leadership not just in terms of what gets accomplished, but how I show up while accomplishing it. Taking responsibility, staying curious, and recognizing when ego or defensiveness is driving a reaction are practical skills, not just personal development concepts.
items.network_core_idea: Awareness precedes choice. Notice your assumptions, emotions, stories, and patterns before they shape your decisions. The prerequisite to better thinking is recognizing that you are part of the system you're trying to understand.
items.teamwork_role: The stance behind the self question: curiosity over being right, responsibility without blame. Separating fact from story is a practice in this book as widely reported.

items.title: Trillion Dollar Coach
items.author: Schmidt, Rosenberg & Eagle
items.card_line: The best leaders spend less time having answers and more time asking good questions and building trust.
items.takeaway_heading: Your job is to make the people around you better
items.takeaway: Trillion Dollar Coach influenced my view of leadership as something less about having all the answers and more about asking good questions, giving honest feedback, building trust, and helping talented people perform at their best.
items.network_core_idea: People perform better when they feel trusted, challenged, and supported. Leadership isn't primarily about having answers. It's about creating the conditions for other people to think, grow, and perform at their best.
items.teamwork_role: Relational moves: honest feedback early, asked before told, trust and challenge together. Governs the step when the person manages the other party.

items.title: What the CEO Wants You to Know
items.author: Ram Charan
items.card_line: Every function lives inside a business. Understanding how value actually gets created makes you better at almost any role.
items.takeaway_heading: Understand the business underneath the job
items.takeaway: This book reinforces how every role exists as an interconnected network, and understanding how that network creates value makes you better at what you do. Knowing your customers, cash flow, margins, and the drivers of profitability helps you see beyond your function and understand how your work contributes to the bigger picture.
items.network_core_idea: Every organization is a system for creating value. Understand customers, revenue, costs, cash, and the basic mechanics of a business. Once you understand how value moves through the organization, your own work becomes part of a larger picture.
items.teamwork_role: The business reading: the other person may be reacting to a number you cannot see.

items.title: Poor Charlie's Almanack
items.author: Charlie Munger
items.card_line: The more disciplines you bring to a problem, the less likely you are to mistake a familiar pattern for the whole picture.
items.takeaway: Poor Charlie's Almanack reinforced my appreciation for mental models and multidisciplinary thinking. The more perspectives you bring to a problem, whether economics, psychology, incentives, statistics, or human behavior, the less likely you are to mistake a familiar pattern for the whole picture.
items.network_core_idea: No single mental model explains reality. Use incentives, inversion, first principles, probability, opportunity cost, and other models to look at the same problem from different angles. The goal isn't to collect frameworks. It's to recognize patterns.
items.teamwork_role: The reason the advisor never settles on one story: more than one model, incentives first, inversion, and the first-conclusion tendency.

items.title: High Output Management
items.author: Andrew S. Grove
items.card_line: Good outcomes shouldn't depend on one person's heroics. Real leverage comes from the systems built around them.
items.takeaway: High Output Management changed how I think about management. Strong outcomes shouldn't depend on one person constantly rescuing a broken process. Good managers create leverage through clear expectations, effective processes, useful metrics, and developing the people around them.
items.network_core_idea: The best results don't always come from doing more. They come from improving the system. Find the bottleneck. Improve the process. Delegate. Multiply the effectiveness of others. Focus your effort where a small intervention can create a much larger outcome.
items.teamwork_role: Output over activity, clear expectations, useful metrics; a process problem often wears a person's face.

where_they_conflict.text: Grove measures a manager by output. The 15 Commitments looks first at how a leader shows up. When someone is delivering and also leaving damage behind, the two give different verdicts.
Candour with care for the person against clear measures kept visible: kind and early feedback can soften a miss that the metric would have shown plainly.
Transparency and trust as the conditions for good work against Munger's warning that incentives quietly override whatever trust was built.
Care for the person against the number the business must hit. The kind thing and the commercial thing differ more often than either book needs to admit.

book.fdt.title: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team
book.fdt.author: Patrick Lencioni
book.fdt.idea: As widely reported: absence of trust, fear of conflict, lack of commitment, avoidance of accountability and inattention to results, each resting on the one before. This book is not in the owner's Reading section and no owner takeaway exists.
book.fdt.use: Only as a way to name a team-level pattern in plain words (silence that looks like agreement, commitments nobody owns). Never attributed to the author on screen, never used to rank anyone.

algorithms.source: decision-os/js/models.js (the functions) and decision-os/js/lessons/index.js (the plain rules each lesson teaches). Teamwork uses the shape of each rule and never its arithmetic: it asks for no probabilities and shows no scores.

items.name: Bayesian updating
items.rule: Start from the base rate. Let each clue move you by how much likelier it is if you are right than if you are wrong. Strong clues move you a lot, cheap talk a little. Nothing moves you to certainty.
items.applies_when: Someone has a belief about another person or a situation and gets a new fact: a reply, a missed meeting, a kind word. The question is how far that fact should move them.
items.trap: Reps under-move on good evidence and over-move on the last thing they heard. At work: one cold email or one warm hallway comment is read as the whole story.
items.flip_point: Taught in the lesson as: a clue three times likelier under 'no' than 'yes' would pull a 75% belief back under 50%.
items.workplace_form: Qualitative only. 'That is one fact and a weak one, because people say it either way' versus 'that is a fact that would be unlikely if your first story were wrong.'

items.name: Value of information
items.rule: Before any check, ask which result would make you do something different, and what that is worth. If no result would, skip the check. A check is valued against the action you are already leaning towards.
items.applies_when: Deciding whether to ask the one question, wait, or gather more before acting.
items.trap: Checks that only confirm what you would do anyway still cost something. The mirror trap: acting without the one cheap check whose answer would flip the move.
items.flip_point: A check breaks even when its cost equals what knowing is worth over deciding now.
items.workplace_form: Ask a question only if each plausible answer leads to a different next step. 'What reason did he give, in his words?' passes. 'How do you feel about it?' usually fails.

items.name: Expected value
items.rule: Chance times prize, minus the cost of chasing it. Rank options by that number, not by the size of the prize.
items.applies_when: Choosing between a large unlikely win and a modest likely one, for example escalating a long shot against fixing a smaller thing that will probably work.
items.trap: Big equals important. A likely small win can be worth about twice an unlikely big one. The cost of your own time is part of the cost.
items.flip_point: Taught in the lesson as the odds at which the big option overtakes the small one (about 23% in the example).
items.workplace_form: Used as a sorting question, never a calculation: how likely is this to work, what is it worth if it does, what does trying cost me. Teamwork never asks a user to put a number on a person.

items.name: Decision tree
items.rule: Lay out the branches, weigh each by its odds, roll the value back to today. Then compare that with what pursuing costs. The branch that carries most of the value is the fact to verify first.
items.applies_when: A choice that depends on one unknown, such as whether the other person has the information or the authority.
items.trap: Precision is less important than order of magnitude, and the tree tells you which uncertainty matters most. Drawing it carefully for a minor uncertainty is wasted care.
items.flip_point: Walk away once the chance of the good branch drops below the point where the expected value no longer covers the cost.
items.workplace_form: The 'what would tell' line on the read screen: the single fact that decides which branch you are on.

items.name: Utility and trade-offs
items.rule: State what you are optimizing for before you compare options. The best option is the best option for a stated objective. When two people disagree on the answer, check whether they disagree on the weights.
items.applies_when: Two people want different things from the same decision: speed against care, results against rest, the standard against the exception.
items.trap: Arguing the options when the real disagreement is the objective. Also: an option that loses on every objective cannot be rescued by any weights.
items.flip_point: Taught in the lesson as the weight at which a second option overtakes the first (about 76% on margin in the example).
items.workplace_form: The 'tension' line: name the two good things pulling against each other and let the person pick the weighting.

items.name: Explore and exploit
items.rule: Spend most of your time where you know it pays. Keep a slice for what you do not understand, sized by how long you will be around to use the answer. Update an estimate, do not replace it, after one bad week.
items.applies_when: A person has settled into a routine with a colleague or manager and has stopped testing whether a different approach would work.
items.trap: Overreacting to the last result in either direction.
items.flip_point: A test pays back if there is enough time left to use what it finds.
items.workplace_form: One small, cheap experiment in the next step, not a campaign.

items.name: Prediction versus decision
items.rule: A forecast tells you what might happen. A decision tells you what to do about it. Break headline numbers into the drivers you can act on, then judge those drivers against the objective.
items.applies_when: Someone says 'this will never change' or 'it will be fine'. Either is a forecast, and neither is a plan.
items.trap: A confident prediction with a bad payoff model produces confident mistakes.
items.flip_point: Not a fixed point; the lesson's example hinges on how much growth is worth against margin.
items.workplace_form: Keep the person's forecast ('he will do it again') apart from their choice ('what I will say on Thursday').

decision_science.name: Base rates
decision_science.idea: Before the details of this case, ask how often situations like it turn out each way. The case in front of you feels unique and most are not.
decision_science.applies_when: The person is sure of a story from one angle ('he always does this', 'this will never get done') and the advisor needs a sober starting point before weighing new facts.
decision_science.misleads_when: There is no honest reference group, or the group is unlike this team. Also when it is used to wave away a person who is describing something that happened: most bosses are fine is no answer to one boss who is not.
decision_science.source: Decision OS, Bayesian Updating lesson ('Start from the base rate').
decision_science.teamwork_use: The advisor may say that a missed deadline has many ordinary causes before it names a motive. It never quotes a percentage, because Teamwork holds no workplace base-rate data.

decision_science.name: Value of information
decision_science.idea: A question is worth asking only if some answer would change what you do. Otherwise the answer is trivia and the asking costs the person energy.
decision_science.applies_when: Deciding whether the advisor asks its one question, and whether the person should find something out before acting.
decision_science.misleads_when: Waiting costs more than knowing is worth (a deadline, a safety issue). Also when asking is itself the right act: 'what reason did you have?' is information and a gesture.
decision_science.source: Decision OS, Value of Information lesson and valueOfInformation(); Friction asks a question only if some answer could change the recommendation.
decision_science.teamwork_use: The question screen appears only when one answer would change the suggestion; otherwise it is skipped.

decision_science.name: Hindsight and outcome bias
decision_science.idea: Once we know how something turned out, we remember having expected it (hindsight), and we judge the decision by its result (outcome bias).
decision_science.applies_when: At the look-back, when the person recalls what they expected after already knowing what happened.
decision_science.misleads_when: Used to dismiss a warning someone actually wrote down at the time. The written line is the guard against the bias, not a casualty of it.
decision_science.source: Widely reported in the judgment-and-decision literature. Not drawn from the owner's material.
decision_science.teamwork_use: The look-back asks two answers from memory before it shows what the person wrote, then shows both so drift is visible.

decision_science.name: The decision versus the result
decision_science.idea: A good decision can end badly and a poor one can end well. Judge the decision by what was known and how it was reasoned. Treat the result as partial evidence about it.
decision_science.applies_when: After a conversation that went badly, or went well by luck, when the person is deciding whether to repeat the approach.
decision_science.misleads_when: It becomes a way never to update. Three similar situations that end the same way are evidence about the approach, not three unlucky draws.
decision_science.source: Widely reported. Decision OS's prediction-versus-decision lesson is a neighbour, not the source.
decision_science.teamwork_use: The inference line at the look-back says what one outcome can and cannot tell. It never says the approach was right or wrong.

decision_science.name: Regression to the mean
decision_science.idea: Extreme days tend to be followed by more ordinary ones with no help from anyone. The worst week and the best week are poor guides to what is typical.
decision_science.applies_when: The person acted right after the worst meeting and things then improved, or reads one terrible interaction as the new normal.
decision_science.misleads_when: Something real changed (a new manager, a reorganization, a promise broken). Then the extreme is a new level, not noise.
decision_science.teamwork_use: A reason to ask how often it happens, not only how bad the last time was, and to avoid crediting the step for a recovery that may have come anyway.

decision_science.name: One observation versus a pattern
decision_science.idea: One event is one draw. A pattern needs several, in different places and at different times. Name the behaviour you saw before you name a trait.
decision_science.applies_when: 'He cut me off twice' is behaviour. 'He doesn't respect me' is a trait inferred from it. The advisor raises an own-part pattern only when the account points at it twice.
decision_science.misleads_when: The first event is serious. A single act of harassment, retaliation or a threat is enough to act on and waiting for a second is the mistake.
decision_science.source: Teamwork's synthesis. The 'twice' threshold is a protocol choice, not a research finding.
decision_science.teamwork_use: Counts on the page are of lines and look-backs, never of people. 'Twice' is the line before an own-part question.

decision_science.name: The fundamental attribution error
decision_science.idea: We tend to explain other people's behaviour by what they are like and our own by what we were up against. The other person is doing the same to us.
decision_science.applies_when: 'She is lazy', 'he is a control freak'. Before the character explanation, ask what the situation would produce in nearly anyone.
decision_science.misleads_when: Treated as a law. Character is sometimes the answer, and how strong this tendency is varies across studies and settings. It is a reason to check the situation, not a reason to rule character out.
decision_science.source: Widely reported social-psychology idea. Decision OS's 'before you explain a person, rule out the situation' case is the owner's reading of the same move.
decision_science.teamwork_use: Standing rule: always carry one explanation that is not about anyone's character.

decision_science.name: Psychological safety
decision_science.idea: People speak up, ask and admit mistakes when they believe it will not cost them. When they do not believe that, silence is a rational reply and not a sign of agreement.
decision_science.applies_when: Problems surface late, everyone agrees in the room and disagrees afterwards, or the person fears raising the issue with the other party.
decision_science.misleads_when: Read as comfort or niceness, or as proof that no one is accountable. It is also not something one person can declare for a team.
decision_science.source: Widely reported (Amy Edmondson's concept). Appears in the owner's reading of How Google Works.
decision_science.teamwork_use: Explains why the fix is often 'make it cheaper to say the true thing' and why the step has to be sized to what the person can safely say.

decision_science.name: Power asymmetry
decision_science.idea: The same sentence costs different people different amounts. The person with less power risks more by speaking, and the person with more often cannot see the cost.
decision_science.applies_when: The other person controls the person's pay, project or reviews, or the person controls theirs. It changes which step is safe, not only which is wise.
decision_science.misleads_when: It makes the person feel they can do nothing, so they skip steps that are within their control. It also hides that managers are constrained from above.
decision_science.source: Teamwork's synthesis from widely reported organizational behaviour. Not in the owner's material, which is mostly written from the manager's seat.
decision_science.teamwork_use: The 'who is this about' answer sets the direction of the advice: upward steps are framed as questions and records, downward steps as expectations.

decision_science.name: Setup problem or person problem
decision_science.idea: Before explaining a person, ask what this setup would produce in almost anyone placed in it: the workload, the number, the unclear owner, the information that never arrived.
decision_science.applies_when: The same thing happens with several people, started when something changed, or follows an incentive or a handoff.
decision_science.misleads_when: One person is the common factor across different setups, or the setup explanation lets real conduct pass. A setup reading no fact could ever test is a story, not an explanation.
decision_science.source: Teamwork's synthesis from the Three Lenses, Friction's states and Decision OS's one-explanation case.
decision_science.teamwork_use: The read screen carries at least one setup explanation, and names the fact that would separate it from the person explanation.

confidence_labels.label: High confidence
confidence_labels.meaning: Several independent answers point the same way and nothing you said cuts against it.

confidence_labels.label: Strong pattern
confidence_labels.meaning: The evidence leans clearly one way. One or two answers could still move it.

confidence_labels.label: Emerging pattern
confidence_labels.meaning: A pattern is forming but a competing explanation is still live. The open question below is how to tell them apart.

confidence_labels.label: Early signal
confidence_labels.meaning: This is the strongest of several weak signals. Treat it as a hypothesis to test, not a finding.

honest_null.name: No clear constraint
honest_null.summary: Your answers didn't point to a constraint.
honest_null.detail: That doesn't rule one out. It means nothing you described rose above a weak signal, and this is a reading of your own answers.
honest_null.mixed_detail: Leaders tend to describe their organizations more favourably than the people who work in them do. That isn't a flaw in you; it is where you sit.
honest_null.next: Ask two or three people the same questions and compare.

rules.name: Happened, told, concluded
rules.text: Keep what happened, what was told and what was concluded apart. Happened counts in full, told at a discount, concluded as a hypothesis.

rules.name: Never diagnose the absent person
rules.text: One account from one side. Describe reported behaviour. Do not assign motives, traits or diagnoses to someone who is not there.

rules.name: Always carry a non-character cause
rules.text: At least one explanation is about the setup, not anyone's character, until facts rule it out.

rules.name: The person's part is a question
rules.text: Raised as a question the person can ask themselves. Never a verdict, never a clean bill.

rules.name: One question, only if it changes the advice
rules.text: Ask nothing if nothing would change. Ask about facts, not judgments.

rules.name: One step, with its assumption, its risk and an alternative
rules.text: A single next move, the words, and honest costs. No menu.

rules.name: Define the outcome before acting
rules.text: One observable sentence and a date, written before the person acts.

rules.name: Honest inference at the look-back
rules.text: One outcome cannot prove an approach worked or failed. Two or three similar situations can start to tell.

rules.name: Say 'can't tell'
rules.text: Uncertainty stated plainly is more useful than confidence invented.

rules.name: Books enter as plain ideas
rules.text: Lightly attributed if at all, never as proof, never quoted, never cited by page.

rules.name: The safety flag
rules.text: Harassment, retaliation, threats, pressure to do something illegal or unsafe: stop giving conversation advice, help record facts, keep copies outside work systems, find who has the duty to act.

rules.name: Plain voice
rules.text: Short sentences, plain words, no jargon, no therapy voice, no em dashes. Speak as a calm, exact colleague.

rules.name: One thing per screen, always a way back and a way to stop
rules.text: Every screen asks one thing. Every screen has a way back and a way to stop that keeps what exists.

trust.knows: Which seat the person says the other party holds. Nothing more.
trust.cannot: How the other person sees the relationship, or whether a seat says anything about fault.
trust.controls: Whether to answer at all. 'Someone else' is always there and Back returns.

links.why: Who holds power over whom decides which next steps are safe, so it is asked before anything else.
The answer names a seat, never a person's character, so nothing here labels the absent party.
One tap on one screen, with a way back and a way to stop that keeps what exists.
This is where a worn-down person lands, so it carries one quiet line and no instruction.
Upward, the person has more to lose by speaking, so later steps lean on questions and written records rather than confrontation.
A manager's reaction decides how costly the truth is to say, so the step is sized to what the person can safely raise.
The owner's reading of Trillion Dollar Coach, asking before telling and honest feedback early, governs the step when the person manages the other party.
A manager gets the five pre-conversation questions before the step.
A manager's output is the team's output, so a report's miss is first read as a possible setup problem the manager helped build.
With no formal power either way, direct candour is more often safe and the step can ask more of the person.
Peers often pull against each other because of what each is measured on, so check the number before the person.
With a group, silence is the thing to read: it is not agreement until someone has been asked what disagreeing would cost.
A quiet team is first a question about whether speaking is safe, not about willingness.
Team-level patterns such as avoided conflict can be named in plain words, widely reported, never attributed or used as a verdict.
A catch-all, so nobody is forced into a box that does not fit. The protocol works without this answer.

steps.title: What's happening?
steps.app: home.what: six patterns and a conduct line.

trust.knows: The line the person picks, as a first guess at the kind of trouble.
trust.cannot: Whether the line fits. Two people can pick the same words for different situations.
trust.controls: Every line can be rewritten on the sort screen. 'Something else' and the conduct line are always there, and quiet by design.

links.why: The first five lines are behaviours that map onto the setup, own-part and team vocabularies, so none of them is a trait.
The last line is a door to the conduct path, which skips the explanations exercise and the openers.
'I think I might be the problem' opens the own-part vocabulary, used as questions only.
Options describe what someone does ('cut me off'), not what someone is.
Missed deadlines have many setup causes (priorities, owners, information) before any character cause, so the system lens is opened first.
People do what the number pays for. Check the incentive before the person.

options.label: They shift the goalposts, then blame me

links.why: 'The goalposts moved' is partly a memory question: after an outcome, both sides remember agreeing to more than they did.
The owner's Grove reading puts clear expectations first, so the first move is what was agreed, in what words, and when.
'Then blame me' is a conclusion; what was said and when is what happened.

options.label: They cut me off or dismiss my ideas

links.why: 'Cut me off' is behaviour seen once or twice; 'dismiss' is a trait inferred from it. The sort screen separates them.
Dismissive is the usual shape of a trait explanation, so a situation explanation is held beside it.
Being cut off by someone senior and by a peer are different events with different safe responses.

options.label: We keep having the same argument

links.why: The same argument again is the Activity Loop in one relationship: motion that does not change what happens next.
The way out is the Learning Loop: a stated expectation and a dated look-back, which is what the rest of the app produces.
One explanation, the first story that fits, is the habit that keeps an argument going.

options.label: I think I might be the problem

links.why: The Awareness force asks what I might be contributing that I cannot see, which is exactly this question.
It leads, but as a question; a non-self explanation is still required so it does not become self-blame.
The owner's reading is that self-awareness is a professional skill, which makes this a reasonable thing to ask and not a confession.
Quiet by design: nothing about the setup is assumed and the sort-and-two-readings protocol works without a category.
Friction's honest null: no category rising above a weak signal is a reading, so the advisor says so rather than forcing one.

options.label: I'm being harassed, or punished for saying no

links.why: Routes straight to the conduct path: facts recorded, copies kept outside work systems, the people with the duty to act.
A single serious act is enough to act on, so waiting for a pattern would be the mistake here.
Retaliation after refusing is a power problem, which is why no conversation advice is offered.

steps.title: What do you need right now?

trust.cannot: Whether it is the right need. Someone asking to prepare may first need to understand.
trust.controls: It changes emphasis, not the steps. Nothing is locked after this tap.

links.why: The five needs sit at different points on the Learning Loop: understanding, decision, action, recovery and the exit.
Whatever the need, the screen sequence ends in one step, not a menu.
Wanting to understand puts the weight on the two readings and the fact that would tell them apart.
Understanding starts by asking what the setup would produce in anyone.
Deciding means stating what you are optimizing for before comparing options.
Judgment is the third stage of the path: weighing, not just seeing.

options.label: To get ready for a conversation

links.why: Preparing for a hard conversation is where the five pre-conversation questions belong, when the person manages the other party.
Widely reported advice from the book is honest and early with care; the words step draws on it.

options.label: To recover from one that went badly

links.why: A conversation that went badly is judged by what was known then, not only by how it ended.
Recovery is where hindsight bends memory hardest, so the sort asks for exact words and times.

options.label: To decide whether to escalate or step away

links.why: Escalating or leaving is a branching choice: what each path would teach you and what each costs.
The cost of each branch depends on who holds power over the outcome.
Escalation can mean the conduct path, so the account is checked for it before any advice.

trust.knows: Only what is typed, word for word.
trust.cannot: Anything it was not told. A short account gives a short sort and the advisor does not pad it.
trust.controls: Skip is always there and nothing is inferred from skipping.

links.why: A line in the person's own words is the raw material for the sort and is carried as written.
Friction always asks about the last time something happened, so the example here is an event with a day and a person.
The help text asks for the way you would say it to a friend, not a report.
A day and a count ('twice on Tuesday') turn 'always' into something checkable.
Events with who and when are what the sort needs most.
Pressing this sends this text for this step only; the server stores nothing and logs no content.
Skipping costs nothing and changes nothing about the rest.

Knowledge comes before understanding: the facts are settled with the person first.

Counts in full: what was said or done, with when and who saw it.
Events weigh more than impressions (1.2 against 0.6 for reassuring impressions in Friction).
Counts at a discount because it reached the person through someone else.
People relaying what someone else is like are explaining by trait too, so told lines about character stay light.
A hypothesis to test, not a fact. 'He doesn't respect me' lives here.
Conclusions about character are the usual shape of the attribution error.
Nothing in this column is carried forward as a claim about the absent person.
