principles.label: Bayesian updating
principles.source: Decision OS, bayesUpdate(prior, evidence)
principles.summary: Start from the base rate. Let each clue move you by how much likelier it is if you are right than if you are wrong. Strong clues move you a lot, cheap talk a little. Nothing moves you to certainty.
principles.applies_when: Someone has a belief about another person or a situation and gets a new fact: a reply, a missed meeting, a kind word. The question is how far that fact should move them.
principles.misleads_when: Reps under-move on good evidence and over-move on the last thing they heard. At work: one cold email or one warm hallway comment is read as the whole story.

principles.label: Value of information
principles.source: Decision OS, valueOfInformation(causes, actions, diagnostics, leaning)
principles.summary: Before any check, ask which result would make you do something different, and what that is worth. If no result would, skip the check. A check is valued against the action you are already leaning towards.
principles.applies_when: Deciding whether to ask the one question, wait, or gather more before acting.
principles.misleads_when: Checks that only confirm what you would do anyway still cost something. The mirror trap: acting without the one cheap check whose answer would flip the move.

principles.label: Expected value
principles.source: Decision OS, expectedValue({p, value, cost})
principles.summary: Chance times prize, minus the cost of chasing it. Rank options by that number, not by the size of the prize.
principles.applies_when: Choosing between a large unlikely win and a modest likely one, for example escalating a long shot against fixing a smaller thing that will probably work.
principles.misleads_when: Big equals important. A likely small win can be worth about twice an unlikely big one. The cost of your own time is part of the cost.

principles.label: Decision tree
principles.source: Decision OS, evaluateTree(node, payoffs)
principles.summary: Lay out the branches, weigh each by its odds, roll the value back to today. Then compare that with what pursuing costs. The branch that carries most of the value is the fact to verify first.
principles.applies_when: A choice that depends on one unknown, such as whether the other person has the information or the authority.
principles.misleads_when: Precision is less important than order of magnitude, and the tree tells you which uncertainty matters most. Drawing it carefully for a minor uncertainty is wasted care.

principles.label: Utility and trade-offs
principles.source: Decision OS, utilityRank(options, weights)
principles.summary: State what you are optimizing for before you compare options. The best option is the best option for a stated objective. When two people disagree on the answer, check whether they disagree on the weights.
principles.applies_when: Two people want different things from the same decision: speed against care, results against rest, the standard against the exception.
principles.misleads_when: Arguing the options when the real disagreement is the objective. Also: an option that loses on every objective cannot be rescued by any weights.

principles.label: Explore and exploit
principles.source: Decision OS, ucbScores(arms, c), allocateHours(arms, hours, c)
principles.summary: Spend most of your time where you know it pays. Keep a slice for what you do not understand, sized by how long you will be around to use the answer. Update an estimate, do not replace it, after one bad week.
principles.applies_when: A person has settled into a routine with a colleague or manager and has stopped testing whether a different approach would work.
principles.misleads_when: Overreacting to the last result in either direction.

principles.label: Prediction versus decision
principles.source: Decision OS, (lesson: prediction-vs-decision)
principles.summary: A forecast tells you what might happen. A decision tells you what to do about it. Break headline numbers into the drivers you can act on, then judge those drivers against the objective.
principles.applies_when: Someone says 'this will never change' or 'it will be fine'. Either is a forecast, and neither is a plan.
principles.misleads_when: A confident prediction with a bad payoff model produces confident mistakes.

principles.label: Base rates
principles.source: Decision OS, Bayesian Updating lesson ('Start from the base rate').
principles.summary: Before the details of this case, ask how often situations like it turn out each way. The case in front of you feels unique and most are not.
principles.applies_when: The person is sure of a story from one angle ('he always does this', 'this will never get done') and the advisor needs a sober starting point before weighing new facts.
principles.misleads_when: There is no honest reference group, or the group is unlike this team. Also when it is used to wave away a person who is describing something that happened: most bosses are fine is no answer to one boss who is not.

principles.label: Value of information
principles.source: Decision OS, Value of Information lesson and valueOfInformation(); Friction asks a question only if some answer could change the recommendation.
principles.summary: A question is worth asking only if some answer would change what you do. Otherwise the answer is trivia and the asking costs the person energy.
principles.applies_when: Deciding whether the advisor asks its one question, and whether the person should find something out before acting.
principles.misleads_when: Waiting costs more than knowing is worth (a deadline, a safety issue). Also when asking is itself the right act: 'what reason did you have?' is information and a gesture.

principles.label: Hindsight and outcome bias
principles.source: Widely reported in the judgment-and-decision literature. Not drawn from the owner's material.
principles.summary: Once we know how something turned out, we remember having expected it (hindsight), and we judge the decision by its result (outcome bias).
principles.applies_when: At the look-back, when the person recalls what they expected after already knowing what happened.
principles.misleads_when: Used to dismiss a warning someone actually wrote down at the time. The written line is the guard against the bias, not a casualty of it.

principles.label: The decision versus the result
principles.source: Widely reported. Decision OS's prediction-versus-decision lesson is a neighbour, not the source.
principles.summary: A good decision can end badly and a poor one can end well. Judge the decision by what was known and how it was reasoned. Treat the result as partial evidence about it.
principles.applies_when: After a conversation that went badly, or went well by luck, when the person is deciding whether to repeat the approach.
principles.misleads_when: It becomes a way never to update. Three similar situations that end the same way are evidence about the approach, not three unlucky draws.

principles.label: Regression to the mean
principles.source: Widely reported statistical idea.
principles.summary: Extreme days tend to be followed by more ordinary ones with no help from anyone. The worst week and the best week are poor guides to what is typical.
principles.applies_when: The person acted right after the worst meeting and things then improved, or reads one terrible interaction as the new normal.
principles.misleads_when: Something real changed (a new manager, a reorganization, a promise broken). Then the extreme is a new level, not noise.

principles.label: One observation versus a pattern
principles.source: Teamwork's synthesis. The 'twice' threshold is a protocol choice, not a research finding.
principles.summary: One event is one draw. A pattern needs several, in different places and at different times. Name the behaviour you saw before you name a trait.
principles.applies_when: 'He cut me off twice' is behaviour. 'He doesn't respect me' is a trait inferred from it. The advisor raises an own-part pattern only when the account points at it twice.
principles.misleads_when: The first event is serious. A single act of harassment, retaliation or a threat is enough to act on and waiting for a second is the mistake.

principles.label: The fundamental attribution error
principles.source: Widely reported social-psychology idea. Decision OS's 'before you explain a person, rule out the situation' case is the owner's reading of the same move.
principles.summary: We tend to explain other people's behaviour by what they are like and our own by what we were up against. The other person is doing the same to us.
principles.applies_when: 'She is lazy', 'he is a control freak'. Before the character explanation, ask what the situation would produce in nearly anyone.
principles.misleads_when: Treated as a law. Character is sometimes the answer, and how strong this tendency is varies across studies and settings. It is a reason to check the situation, not a reason to rule character out.

principles.label: Psychological safety
principles.source: Widely reported (Amy Edmondson's concept). Appears in the owner's reading of How Google Works.
principles.summary: People speak up, ask and admit mistakes when they believe it will not cost them. When they do not believe that, silence is a rational reply and not a sign of agreement.
principles.applies_when: Problems surface late, everyone agrees in the room and disagrees afterwards, or the person fears raising the issue with the other party.
principles.misleads_when: Read as comfort or niceness, or as proof that no one is accountable. It is also not something one person can declare for a team.

principles.label: Power asymmetry
principles.source: Teamwork's synthesis from widely reported organizational behaviour. Not in the owner's material, which is mostly written from the manager's seat.
principles.summary: The same sentence costs different people different amounts. The person with less power risks more by speaking, and the person with more often cannot see the cost.
principles.applies_when: The other person controls the person's pay, project or reviews, or the person controls theirs. It changes which step is safe, not only which is wise.
principles.misleads_when: It makes the person feel they can do nothing, so they skip steps that are within their control. It also hides that managers are constrained from above.

principles.label: Setup problem or person problem
principles.source: Teamwork's synthesis from the Three Lenses, Friction's states and Decision OS's one-explanation case.
principles.summary: Before explaining a person, ask what this setup would produce in almost anyone placed in it: the workload, the number, the unclear owner, the information that never arrived.
principles.applies_when: The same thing happens with several people, started when something changed, or follows an incentive or a handoff.
principles.misleads_when: One person is the common factor across different setups, or the setup explanation lets real conduct pass. A setup reading no fact could ever test is a story, not an explanation.

principles.label: Events outweigh impressions
principles.source: Friction, js/content.js and js/engine.js
principles.summary: Reassuring answers about a general impression count for less than reassuring answers about something that happened; admissions about your own part count more.

principles.label: Fifteen setup states
principles.source: Friction, js/content.js and js/engine.js
principles.summary: A vocabulary for naming what in the setup might be producing the friction: direction, economics, capability, trust, loss, pressure, focus, information, decision rights, conflict avoidance, blame, centralization, execution, leverage, talent.

principles.label: Ask only if an answer could change the advice
principles.source: Friction, js/content.js and js/engine.js
principles.summary: Friction simulates each answer and asks only when one could change the recommendation.

principles.label: Always ask for the last time it happened
principles.source: Friction, js/content.js and js/engine.js
principles.summary: Seven questions are always asked before the engine may stop; six of them are about an event.

principles.label: Confidence is a label, not a number
principles.source: Friction, js/content.js and js/engine.js
principles.summary: High confidence, Strong pattern, Emerging pattern, Early signal: each with a plain sentence about what it does and does not mean.

principles.label: The honest null
principles.source: Friction, js/content.js and js/engine.js
principles.summary: 'Your answers didn't point to a constraint' does not rule one out; ask other people the same questions and compare.

principles.label: The outcome step lets the read change
principles.source: Friction, js/content.js and js/engine.js
principles.summary: After an experiment, Improved, No change or Worse is compared with what was predicted and the read can move.

principles.label: Commit before you see
principles.source: Decision OS, scenarios3.js and the Learn lessons
principles.summary: Commit before you see. Write the call, then see the reasoning. In Teamwork: The blind look-back and the written expectation.

principles.label: One pause question before the choice, asked of yourself
principles.source: Decision OS, scenarios3.js and the Learn lessons
principles.summary: One pause question before the choice, asked of yourself. In Teamwork: The self question on the read screen.

principles.label: Five questions a manager asks before a hard performance conversation
principles.source: Decision OS, scenarios3.js and the Learn lessons
principles.summary: Five questions a manager asks before a hard performance conversation. In Teamwork: The manager questions on the step screen.

principles.label: Every management case is two good values pulling apart, with the lesson behind the strong move and the lesson pulling the other way
principles.source: Decision OS, scenarios3.js and the Learn lessons
principles.summary: Every management case is two good values pulling apart, with the lesson behind the strong move and the lesson pulling the other way. In Teamwork: The tension line on the read screen.

principles.label: Eight habit families: rescuing, avoiding, controlling, pleasing, over-promising, defending, grinding, one explanation
principles.source: Decision OS, scenarios3.js and the Learn lessons
principles.summary: Eight habit families: rescuing, avoiding, controlling, pleasing, over-promising, defending, grinding, one explanation. In Teamwork: Own-part questions, raised only when the account points at one twice.

principles.label: Delayed kindness is a loan she repays with interest.
principles.source: Decision OS, Module 3 case 'loved-not-delivering' (owner's reading of: Trillion Dollar Coach)
principles.summary: Compare commit and actual for every rep. Book the talk.
principles.pause: Who should tell Dana: you now, or your director in January?
principles.tension: Useful metrics keep misses visible.

principles.label: What you allow in your best rep becomes everyone's rule.
principles.source: Decision OS, Module 3 case 'top-rep-cuts-corners' (owner's reading of: High Output Management)
principles.summary: Walk three “executed” displays you haven't seen.
principles.pause: What will the team learn from your next move?
principles.tension: Honest feedback only works inside trust.

principles.label: A standard with a reason survives its first bad Friday.
principles.source: Decision OS, Module 3 case 'inherited-slack-habits' (owner's reading of: High Output Management)
principles.summary: Pick one inherited routine. Cut every unused field.
principles.pause: Could you explain this rule, or only enforce it?
principles.tension: Give people context to decide.

principles.label: A rule only your best person can skip is a perk.
principles.source: Decision OS, Module 3 case 'exception-request' (owner's reading of: High Output Management)
principles.summary: Ask each rep: what is Monday's call for?
principles.pause: Would your answer change for a middle performer?
principles.tension: Autonomy and context let strong people act.

principles.label: Say what you've seen, then ask what's changed.
principles.source: Decision OS, Module 3 case 'veteran-gone-quiet' (owner's reading of: Trillion Dollar Coach)
principles.summary: Book a long lunch with the person who changed.
principles.pause: What would Ray want you to ask him?
principles.tension: Stay curious; your story may be a reaction.

principles.label: Ask what someone needs before deciding what's kind.
principles.source: Decision OS, Module 3 case 'spouse-is-ill' (owner's reading of: The 15 Commitments of Conscious Leadership)
principles.summary: Learn today what leave and flexible-schedule options exist.
principles.pause: What do you know Tom needs, and what do you assume?
principles.tension: Transparency helps a team decide together.

principles.label: How you hold a friend to a rule shows your word's worth.
principles.source: Decision OS, Module 3 case 'promoted-over-friend' (owner's reading of: The 15 Commitments of Conscious Leadership)
principles.summary: List the three people you go easiest on. Book one talk.
principles.pause: Which costs more: some friendship, or the team's belief you're fair?
principles.tension: Honest feedback builds trust, even between friends.

principles.label: Be honest soonest with those you depend on most.
principles.source: Decision OS, Module 3 case 'distributor-rep-slipped' (owner's reading of: Trillion Dollar Coach)
principles.summary: Learn what's on your key distributor reps' plates first.
principles.pause: What do you owe someone you depend on and underpay?
principles.tension: Know how the other side makes money.

principles.label: A vague promise is a debt. Pay it with specifics.
principles.source: Decision OS, Module 3 case 'ready-for-promotion' (owner's reading of: Trillion Dollar Coach)
principles.summary: List every “next cycle” you've said. Make each a date or a no.
principles.pause: What did Lena hear in “next cycle”? What did you mean?
principles.tension: Take responsibility for your part.

principles.label: Weekly fixes are a process problem, not a favor.
principles.source: Decision OS, Module 3 case 'you-keep-rescuing' (owner's reading of: High Output Management)
principles.summary: List the last five things you fixed. Write a checklist for the commonest.
principles.pause: Whose proposal is this, and what does the team learn?
principles.tension: Helping people perform can mean being slower today.

principles.label: One-person dependence isn't loyalty. It's a risk he carries alone.
principles.source: Decision OS, Module 3 case 'hero-holds-the-account' (owner's reading of: High Output Management)
principles.summary: List your five biggest accounts and who else could run each.
principles.pause: Is it loyal to leave him carrying this alone?
principles.tension: Trust built over years earns the right to ask for more.

principles.label: People do what the number pays for. Fix yours first.
principles.source: Decision OS, Module 3 case 'metrics-reward-the-wrong-thing' (owner's reading of: What the CEO Wants You to Know)
principles.summary: For each number you pay on, ask how a clever rep could game it.
principles.pause: What does telling your director now risk, and what does waiting risk?
principles.tension: Pay shapes behavior; bring psychology and economics.

principles.label: Give context and a limit, not permission case by case.
principles.source: Decision OS, Module 3 case 'context-not-permission' (owner's reading of: How Google Works)
principles.summary: Ask a rep what they skipped for fear of not being allowed.
principles.pause: What are you protecting by approving $900?
principles.tension: Useful metrics let you check what was decided.

principles.label: Trust the person, check the work, check everyone alike.
principles.source: Decision OS, Module 3 case 'says-all-set' (owner's reading of: Trillion Dollar Coach)
principles.summary: Pick one status you accept on someone's word. Spot-check it.
principles.pause: Can you check his work without him hearing that you doubt him?
principles.tension: Clear expectations and useful metrics apply to everyone.

principles.label: Confidence is a feeling. Evidence is what the buyer did.
principles.source: Decision OS, Module 3 case 'lock-that-isnt' (owner's reading of: Poor Charlie's Almanack)
principles.summary: Tally each rep's “locks” against closes. Show them quarterly.
principles.pause: Would Dave bet his own money on it?
principles.tension: Building trust helps talented people do their best.

principles.label: Silence isn't agreement. Ask what disagreeing with you costs.
principles.source: Decision OS, Module 3 case 'team-agrees' (owner's reading of: How Google Works)
principles.summary: Ask “what's the weakest part of this plan?” and wait.
principles.pause: What does disagreeing with you cost a rep?
principles.tension: More perspectives keep you from missing the whole picture.

principles.label: Before you explain a person, rule out the situation.
principles.source: Decision OS, Module 3 case 'one-explanation' (owner's reading of: Poor Charlie's Almanack)
principles.summary: When numbers move, list three causes that aren't the person.
principles.pause: What would you see if it weren't effort?
principles.tension: Stay curious; notice when ego writes the story.

principles.label: Tired is a business risk. Protect rest like a key account.
principles.source: Decision OS, Module 3 case 'q4-fatigue' (owner's reading of: The 15 Commitments of Conscious Leadership)
principles.summary: Block next week's non-negotiables first: sleep, one evening, one meal.
principles.pause: What would you tell a friend running on five hours' sleep?
principles.tension: A team with context can carry some of the load.

principles.label: Own it in one sentence before you explain it.
principles.source: Decision OS, Module 3 case 'defensive-in-review' (owner's reading of: The 15 Commitments of Conscious Leadership)
principles.summary: Write the one sentence you'd say after a miss.
principles.pause: What would your best rep say first?
principles.tension: A good leader welcomes honest feedback.

principles.label: Keep what you love, and use it to make someone better.
principles.source: Decision OS, Module 3 case 'miss-the-field' (owner's reading of: High Output Management)
principles.summary: Book the two overdue one-on-ones first.
principles.pause: Who pays when your hours go to what you love?
principles.tension: How you show up matters; notice what drives you.

principles.label: Rest works when the team knows who decides.
principles.source: Decision OS, Module 3 case 'vacation-text' (owner's reading of: How Google Works)
principles.summary: Before time off, write who decides what and who covers.
principles.pause: If you never replied, who would decide?
principles.tension: Notice whether your reaction serves the work or your ego.

principles.label: When you're most sure, look hardest for how you're wrong.
principles.source: Decision OS, Module 3 case 'sure-of-the-plan' (owner's reading of: Poor Charlie's Almanack)
principles.summary: Before a big plan, write what you'd see in 30 days if wrong.
principles.pause: What would show you were wrong in 30 days?
principles.tension: Ask good questions so the team can improve the plan.

principles.label: Ask what a deadline is for before giving up a weekend.
principles.source: Decision OS, Module 3 case 'friday-6pm-email' (owner's reading of: The 15 Commitments of Conscious Leadership)
principles.summary: When a deadline lands late, ask what decision it supports.
principles.pause: What is the deadline for? Do you know?
principles.tension: Context helps people decide, and a request's purpose is context.

principles.label: Bad news worsens weekly. Bring the range, the drivers, the ask.
principles.source: Decision OS, Module 3 case 'number-you-cant-hit' (owner's reading of: What the CEO Wants You to Know)
principles.summary: Write today's honest range and its drivers. Send it first.
principles.pause: What would your VP want to know, and when?
principles.tension: Notice fear or defensiveness before it writes your answer.

principles.label: Say what you can and can't. Never say what isn't so.
principles.source: Decision OS, Module 3 case 'reorg-rumor' (owner's reading of: How Google Works)
principles.summary: Write three sentences: what you can say, can't, and when you'll update.
principles.pause: Will they remember what you said, or that you said it?
principles.tension: Think through what each person will do when they hear it.

principles.label: A win that costs another team isn't yet the company's win.
principles.source: Decision OS, Module 3 case 'win-that-costs-supply' (owner's reading of: What the CEO Wants You to Know)
principles.summary: Before closing a big deal, ask who else needs what it uses.
principles.pause: Whose call is it which one runs?
principles.tension: Share context early so affected people can decide with you.

principles.label: Whoever made the promise fixes it, with you beside them.
principles.source: Decision OS, Module 3 case 'rookie-overpromises' (owner's reading of: Trillion Dollar Coach)
principles.summary: Write three questions to ask before promising a date or display.
principles.pause: Whose call is this, and who learns most from it?
principles.tension: Clear expectations keep outcomes from depending on one person.

principles.label: A rep who says “fine” five times is telling you something.
principles.source: Decision OS, Module 3 case 'quiet-says-fine' (owner's reading of: Trillion Dollar Coach)
principles.summary: Ask a rep you've only asked “how are you?”: “What's the least fun part of your week?”
principles.pause: What haven't you asked because you fear the answer?
principles.tension: Stay curious about what you have avoided asking.

principles.label: Ask first, answer second, and only if they're stuck.
principles.source: Decision OS, Module 3 case 'ask-dont-answer' (owner's reading of: Trillion Dollar Coach)
principles.summary: Next five times he asks, answer “what do you think?” first.
principles.pause: Which would Ben remember: your answer, or his?
principles.tension: Develop people so your time reaches further.

principles.label: Celebrate results, not hours.
principles.source: Decision OS, Module 3 case 'burned-out-star' (owner's reading of: Trillion Dollar Coach)
principles.summary: Check the timestamps on your team's emails and yours.
principles.pause: What are you teaching the team about what you notice?
principles.tension: Take responsibility for how your own reactions land, praise included.

principles.label: Rescuing
principles.source: Decision OS, families3
principles.summary: You step in and fix it, or give the answer before you have asked. It works today and teaches the team to wait for you.

principles.label: Avoiding
principles.source: Decision OS, families3
principles.summary: You wait, soften, or hand it off. The conversation you skip is usually the one that matters.

principles.label: Controlling
principles.source: Decision OS, families3
principles.summary: You reach for a rule, a check or a consequence where a conversation would do.

principles.label: Pleasing
principles.source: Decision OS, families3
principles.summary: You protect how people feel about you, or decide what they can handle.

principles.label: Over-promising
principles.source: Decision OS, families3
principles.summary: You commit, or cheer a commitment, past what the evidence supports.

principles.label: Defending
principles.source: Decision OS, families3
principles.summary: You explain or point elsewhere before saying what is yours.

principles.label: Grinding
principles.source: Decision OS, families3
principles.summary: You answer pressure with more hours and call it dedication.

principles.label: One explanation
principles.source: Decision OS, families3
principles.summary: You settle on the first story that fits and stop looking.

principles.label: Standards
principles.source: Decision OS, skills3
principles.summary: Say what good looks like, and hold it for everyone.

principles.label: Candor
principles.source: Decision OS, skills3
principles.summary: Say the true thing, early, and kindly.

principles.label: Systems
principles.source: Decision OS, skills3
principles.summary: Build it so results don't depend on a hero.

principles.label: Trust and verify
principles.source: Decision OS, skills3
principles.summary: Give trust freely. Check what matters, the same way for everyone.

principles.label: Leading yourself
principles.source: Decision OS, skills3
principles.summary: Own your reactions, your fears and your rest.

principles.label: Up and across
principles.source: Decision OS, skills3
principles.summary: Carry the truth up, the context down, and a fair view sideways.

principles.label: Growing people
principles.source: Decision OS, skills3
principles.summary: Ask first. Help them get better, not just get it done.

principles.label: Happened, told, concluded
principles.source: Teamwork protocol, standing rule 1 (server/protocol.md)
principles.summary: Keep what happened, what was told and what was concluded apart. Happened counts in full, told at a discount, concluded as a hypothesis.

principles.label: Never diagnose the absent person
principles.source: Teamwork protocol, standing rule 2 (server/protocol.md)
principles.summary: One account from one side. Describe reported behaviour. Do not assign motives, traits or diagnoses to someone who is not there.

principles.label: Always carry a non-character cause
principles.source: Teamwork protocol, standing rule 3 (server/protocol.md)
principles.summary: At least one explanation is about the setup, not anyone's character, until facts rule it out.

principles.label: The person's part is a question
principles.source: Teamwork protocol, standing rule 4 (server/protocol.md)
principles.summary: Raised as a question the person can ask themselves. Never a verdict, never a clean bill.

principles.label: One question, only if it changes the advice
principles.source: Teamwork protocol, standing rule 5 (server/protocol.md)
principles.summary: Ask nothing if nothing would change. Ask about facts, not judgments.

principles.label: One step, with its assumption, its risk and an alternative
principles.source: Teamwork protocol, standing rule 6 (server/protocol.md)
principles.summary: A single next move, the words, and honest costs. No menu.

principles.label: Define the outcome before acting
principles.source: Teamwork protocol, standing rule 7 (server/protocol.md)
principles.summary: One observable sentence and a date, written before the person acts.

principles.label: Honest inference at the look-back
principles.source: Teamwork protocol, standing rule 8 (server/protocol.md)
principles.summary: One outcome cannot prove an approach worked or failed. Two or three similar situations can start to tell.

principles.label: Say 'can't tell'
principles.source: Teamwork protocol, standing rule 9 (server/protocol.md)
principles.summary: Uncertainty stated plainly is more useful than confidence invented.

principles.label: Books enter as plain ideas
principles.source: Teamwork protocol, standing rule 10 (server/protocol.md)
principles.summary: Lightly attributed if at all, never as proof, never quoted, never cited by page.

principles.label: The safety flag
principles.source: Teamwork protocol, standing rule 11 (server/protocol.md)
principles.summary: Harassment, retaliation, threats, pressure to do something illegal or unsafe: stop giving conversation advice, help record facts, keep copies outside work systems, find who has the duty to act.

principles.label: Plain voice
principles.source: Teamwork protocol, standing rule 12 (server/protocol.md)
principles.summary: Short sentences, plain words, no jargon, no therapy voice, no em dashes. Speak as a calm, exact colleague.

principles.label: One thing per screen, always a way back and a way to stop
principles.source: Teamwork CLAUDE.md rules; one-thing and counts rules follow Stillward's practice
principles.summary: Every screen asks one thing. Every screen has a way back and a way to stop that keeps what exists.

principles.label: Counts, never scores
principles.source: Teamwork CLAUDE.md rules; one-thing and counts rules follow Stillward's practice
principles.summary: Counts only grow. No streaks, no reminders from us, no score on a person or on the user.

principles.label: It stays in this browser
principles.source: Teamwork CLAUDE.md rules; one-thing and counts rules follow Stillward's practice
principles.summary: The server stores nothing and logs no content. The only copy is the person's.

principles.label: Ram Dass: "The quieter you become, the more you can hear."
principles.source: Stillward, as attributed there. Not workplace evidence.
principles.summary: The first screen, for someone who arrives worn down. One line, no instruction attached.

principles.label: Peter Crone: "Awareness is the beginning of change."
principles.source: Stillward, as attributed there. Not workplace evidence.
principles.summary: After the person has chosen a step and written what they expect, as relief from having to solve everything at once.

principles.label: A.H. Almaas: "Inquiry is not a technique. It is a way of being."
principles.source: Stillward, as attributed there. Not workplace evidence.
principles.summary: Before the blind answers, when memory is most likely to bend towards the result. It asks for curiosity about what happened, not a verdict.

principles.label: The done screen's feelings, with honest exits
principles.source: Stillward, done screen (Lighter, Calmer, Clearer, Tender, Unchanged, Still heavy)
principles.summary: A feeling is kept as a feeling, never scored, and the honest negative answer opens exits instead of a nudge.
